newsitem.title: USA: Mexican citizen seeks stay of Texas execution.
newsitem.headline: Mexican citizen seeks stay of Texas execution.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court and Texas prison officials on Monday weighed a final round of appeals from a Mexican citizen set to be executed in Texas this week for his role in a 1985 murder, officials said.
An attorney for the condemned man, Irineo Tristan Montoya, also was preparing an eleventh-hour appeal to the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals seeking to delay Wednesday's scheduled execution.

If the appeals fail, Tristan on Tuesday will begin a routine suicide watch 36 hours before he is strapped to a gurney and executed by lethal injection at the Huntsville State Prison, a prison spokesman said.

"If they are going to kill me, I'd want them to do it once and for all. I don't want to spend another five years in here only for them to kill me anyway," Tristan said in a recent death row interview.

Tristan is one of three people scheduled to be put to death this week in Texas, and his pending execution has drawn little notice in a state which has carried out a record 22 death sentences so far this year.

But the case has sparked strong protests by Mexican officials and prompted a diplomatic inquiry from the U.S. State Department, which asked the Texas governor to investigate whether Tristan's rights as a Mexican citizen were violated after he was arrested on murder charges in Brownsville, Texas.
Tristan was convicted of murder in the November 1985 death of John Kilheffer, who was stabbed at least 22 times and his body dumped in a grapefruit grove near the Texas-Mexico border.

In a confession, Tristan said he and another man, Juan Villavicencio, were picked up by Kilheffer while hitchhiking. Tristan said Villavicencio stabbed Kilheffer after he asked the men if they wanted to go to a motel to have sex, prosecutors said.
Tristan was convicted and sentenced to die for his role in the killing. Villavicencio was tried for capital murder and acquitted in a separate trial, prosecutors said.
Tristan's attorney argued his confession should have been thrown out because he was not informed of his right to contact Mexican consular officials when he was arrested.
